title: Product Hunt and Show HN Launch Rules: What the Pages Say and a 4-Week Prep Plan
title_hi: Product Hunt and Show HN Launch Rules: What the Pages Say and a 4-Week Prep Plan
summary: Two of the most popular places to launch a side project publish their rules in plain language. Almost nobody reads them
content:
Two of the most popular places to launch a side project publish their rules in plain language. Almost nobody reads them before launch day, and both rule sets are short enough to read over a coffee.

I read them again this week. The interesting part is not any single rule. It is that the two platforms, built for different audiences, land on the same handful of constraints, and those constraints tell you exactly how to spend the four weeks before you launch.


  
  
  What the Show HN page says


Show HN's own guidelines open with the test: "Show HN is for something you've made that other people can play with." Then they list what does not qualify, in the page's words: "blog posts, sign-up pages, newsletters, lists, and other reading material. Those can't be tried out."

Three more lines matter for anyone planning a launch:


"Please make it easy for users to try your thing out, ideally without barriers such as signups or emails."
"Don't post landing pages or fundraisers."
"Please don't ask friends to upvote or comment. That's not ok on HN."


So the unit of a Show HN launch is a working thing a stranger can use in under a minute, with no gate in front of it. A waitlist page fails the first test before anyone reads your title.


  
  
  What the Product Hunt page says


Product Hunt's launch guide is stricter about who you are and softer about when. The page states that "Company accounts are prohibited", so a launch runs from a personal account. It says launching is "100% free to use", that you can launch "as often as you have new significant product iterations", and that there is "no discernible advantage to using a third-party hunter", so you can self-hunt.

On timing, the guidance is that "12:01 am Pacific Time is the best time to launch for makers that are planning ahead", followed straight away by "The best day to launch is the day on which you're most prepared."

On help from friends, it is direct: don't ask directly for upvotes. The page tells makers to ask people to "visit and comment" instead.


  
  
  The pattern under both rule sets


Put the two side by side and the shared logic is easy to see.



Both ban the shortcut. Neither wants a launch that is mostly an audience pressed into voting. The rules are written against manufactured momentum.

Both reward a thing that can be used. HN wants something people can try. Product Hunt's own wording about significant iterations points the same way: a real change, not a re-announcement.

Both leave a legitimate door open. HN welcomes curious questions and specific feedback. Product Hunt says to invite visits and comments. What is left after the shortcuts are removed is real attention from real people.


That is the useful reading. The rules do not say "do not get help". They say the help has to look like what it is: someone looked at your product and told you something true about it.


  
  
  What to do with the four weeks before launch


If the rules push everything toward real use and real comments, then the work before launch day is collecting the people who will give you both, and it has to happen before the clock starts, because the launch day itself is too late to recruit.

Week 4: get the thing usable with no gate. Remove the signup wall from the first experience. If a stranger cannot get a result in a minute, HN is closed to you and Product Hunt visitors will bounce.

Week 3: get five strangers to use it and write down what they say. Not friends who will be kind. Their sentences become your first comments, your launch copy, and your list of what to fix.

Week 2: fix what they hit, then ask for specific feedback, not votes. "Tell me where this confused you" is a request you can make in public. "Please upvote" is the request both platforms wrote a rule about.

Week 1: line up people who will visit and comment honestly on the day. This is the step most solo builders skip, and it is the only one that cannot be done alone.


  
  
  The bit that is hard to do alone


That last step is where a solo founder runs out of road. You have no team to send a message to. Your friends are precisely the group the rules warn you off. So the supply of honest early comments comes from people who are also launching and who know what a useful comment looks like.

That is the reason I built Favors.dev. Founders help each other's launches with a testimonial, a share, or real feedback, earn verified points for the work, and spend those points to bring people to their own launch. Points are earned by doing the work, not bought, and the work is verified before points release. If you point the help at feedback and comments rather than votes, it sits inside what both rule pages describe. Read the rules of whichever platform you launch on and ask for the kind of help they permit.


  
  
  Before you launch anywhere



Read the rules page of the exact platform, the week before, not the night before.
Make the first minute of use gate-free.
Get five honest strangers on the thing while there is still time to fix what they find.
Ask for visits, comments and specific feedback. Never for votes.
Collect the people who will show up on launch day before launch day.


If you have launched on either platform, tell me which rule surprised you most. And if you want a place to swap ideas with other builders, come and say hello in the Vibe Coding is Life community on Skool.

title: Your missed-call text-back is not firing: six things that break it
title_hi: Your missed-call text-back is not firing: six things that break it
summary: The dashboard says the message sent. The customer never got it. That gap has a small number of causes, and they are wort
content:
The dashboard says the message sent. The customer never got it. That gap has a small number of causes, and they are worth ruling out in a specific order.


  
  
  The shape of the problem


A missed-call text-back is a short chain, and a break anywhere in it looks identical from the outside: the call comes in, nobody picks up, and no text arrives. Your software usually reports success, because from its point of view it did everything it was asked to do.

That is why guessing is expensive here. The six causes below are ordered by how often they turn out to be the answer, and the first one accounts for most of the silent failures.


  
  
  1. Carrier registration is missing or was rejected


US carriers require application-to-person messaging sent from a standard ten-digit number to be registered: a brand, and a campaign describing what you send and how people consented. Unregistered traffic is filtered or blocked rather than returned with an error.

This is the failure mode that wastes the most time, because nothing in your own tooling looks wrong. The send succeeded. The handoff succeeded. The message simply stopped at the carrier. If your text-back worked at some point and then quietly stopped, check whether a campaign lapsed or was rejected before you check anything else.


Worth knowing

Registration is a carrier requirement, not a law. There is usually no fine attached. The penalty is that your messages do not arrive, which for a lead-capture automation is the entire cost.



  
  
  2. A previous STOP is still suppressing that number


If a specific customer never gets your text-back while everyone else does, look for a revocation. Someone who once replied STOP to any of your messaging, including a campaign unrelated to this one, will usually sit on a permanent suppression list.

This is working as intended and you should not try to route around it. Consent revocation has to be honored, and the rules give you a limited window to act on it. The right response is to recognize it as the cause and stop debugging, not to find a way to message that person anyway.


  
  
  3. The trigger is listening to the wrong call outcome


A missed call is not one event. Declining on your handset, letting it ring out, forwarding to voicemail, answering and immediately dropping, and a call that never reaches your device at all can all be distinct outcomes to whatever is watching the line.

Plenty of setups are wired to one of those and not the others, which produces the most confusing version of this problem: it works sometimes. If yours fires for some real calls and not others, this is usually why.


Test each outcome separately rather than testing once and declaring it working.
Check whether calls that go through a forwarding chain still register as missed on the instrumented number.
Confirm the automation is watching the number customers actually dial, not a secondary line.
## 4. Business-hours logic is suppressing it


Many setups ship with a schedule, and the default is often business hours. That quietly removes the automation from exactly the window it was bought for: evenings, weekends, and the hours when the person who normally answers is asleep.

A missed call at eight on a Saturday evening is not a lower-value lead than one at eleven on a Tuesday. It is usually a higher-value one, because fewer competitors are picking up. Check the schedule before you assume the automation is broken, because a schedule doing its job looks exactly like a failure.


  
  
  5. The number is not text-enabled, or is the wrong type


A traditional landline cannot send or receive SMS unless it has been text-enabled. That is a single setting somewhere, and it is invisible until you try to use it.

Beyond that, number types are treated differently by carriers. Toll-free numbers, ten-digit long codes, and short codes each have their own registration path and their own filtering behaviour. Using the wrong one for your volume and use case tends to produce inconsistent delivery rather than total failure, which is harder to spot.


  
  
  6. The message body is getting filtered


Carriers filter on content as well as registration. Messages that read like unsolicited marketing, lean heavily on shortened links, or use formatting associated with spam can be dropped even from a properly registered campaign.

For a text-back this is easy to avoid, because the message that performs best is also the message least likely to be filtered: short, plainly identifying your business, referring to the call that just happened, and asking a question. Keeping promotional content out of it helps on this front and on the compliance front at the same time.


  
  
  The order to check, and when to stop



Confirm carrier registration is active and the campaign was approved.
Check whether the affected number is on a suppression list.
Test every missed-call outcome separately, not just the one that is easy to reproduce.
Read the schedule, including timezone.
Confirm the sending number is text-enabled and the right type for the use case.
Simplify the message body and retest.


If you have been through all six and it still does not fire reliably, the honest read is that you are now maintaining infrastructure rather than running a business. That is the point at which a managed setup stops being a convenience and starts being the cheaper option, because the cost of a text-back that silently does not work is every lead it was supposed to catch.


  
  
  Questions this post answers


Why does my missed-call text-back say sent but never arrive?

Almost always carrier filtering. US carriers require application-to-person traffic from a ten-digit number to be registered with a brand and a campaign, and unregistered or rejected traffic gets dropped rather than bounced. Your software reports a successful handoff because it did hand off. The message just never made it past the carrier.

Why does it work when I test it but not for real customers?

Two common reasons. You may be testing from a number that is already on an allowlist or has messaged you before, and you may be testing a call outcome that differs from a real one. A call you decline on your handset, a call that forwards to voicemail, and a call that rings out can be three different events to the automation, and only some of them may be wired to the trigger.

Can an old STOP reply block future texts to that customer?

Yes, and it should. Once someone revokes consent you have to honor it, and most platforms keep a permanent suppression list so you cannot accidentally message them again. If one specific customer never receives your text-back, check whether they ever replied STOP to anything you sent, including a different campaign.

Does the number I send from matter?

It matters a lot. A landline that has not been text-enabled cannot receive or send SMS at all, and toll-free, ten-digit long code, and short code numbers are registered and filtered differently. Sending from the wrong number type for your use case is a common cause of messages that deliver inconsistently rather than not at all.

How fast should the text actually go out?

Fast enough to beat the next contractor on the list, which in practice means seconds rather than minutes. The value of a text-back decays quickly, because the caller is still holding their phone. If yours is arriving several minutes later, treat that as a failure to fix rather than a quirk to live with.

  How Sherlock AI Face Search Works


Whichever version you use, Sherlock is a reverse face search: it looks for the same face in different photos, not copies of the same picture. That's what separates it from Google Lens or TinEye. The flow looks like this:



You upload a photo of one face. The apps ask for a single, clear face. Some let you crop the face out of a larger picture first.

The photo goes to a face search engine. Sherlock Search says outright that your photo is sent to "our search provider" to run the search. Neither of the two web versions we checked names that provider.

The face is matched against public pages. Both web versions list the same kinds of sources: Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, X, LinkedIn, YouTube, Pinterest, OnlyFans and the wider public web (Sherlock Search also lists public records).

You get ranked possible matches. Results come back as profiles and pages ranked by how closely the face matches. Seeing all of them usually needs a paid plan.


Sherlock Search also spells out the limit that applies to every tool like this: it only searches what's already public. It doesn't log into accounts, read private messages or reach anything behind a password. A private profile, or a face no engine has indexed, won't turn up.   What Sherlock Costs


Neither web version lists prices on its home page — the price appears at checkout. What their terms do say is how billing works:



Sherlockapp.com: trial plans convert automatically to the monthly membership shown at checkout unless you cancel by 11:59 PM Pacific Time on the trial's last day. Memberships renew until cancelled, and searches from the trial don't carry over.

Sherlock Search: subscriptions renew until cancelled, and you manage them on the platform you bought through, such as the App Store.

Store apps: most sell weekly or monthly subscriptions. Recent App Store reviews of one "Sherlock: AI Face Search" app mention weekly plans around $9 with a small number of searches each week.


A subscription makes sense if you'll run searches every week. If you want to check one dating match or one seller, a weekly plan you forget to cancel can cost far more than the check was worth.





  
  
  Is Sherlock AI Face Search Safe?


Nothing we found suggests the two web versions are scams. They publish terms, privacy statements and support contacts. "Safe" has several parts, though, and they differ by version:










What happens to your upload
Sherlockapp.com says your photo is used only to run your search and is never added to a public index or sold. Sherlock Search says the photo goes to its search provider and isn't stored on its own servers.


Who you're dealing with
Sherlock Search names BZHAPPS as its operator. Sherlockapp.com gives a support email but no company name. Store apps each have their own developer — check which one before you pay.


Billing
Subscriptions renew automatically. On Sherlockapp.com a trial turns into a monthly membership unless you cancel by 11:59 PM Pacific on the trial's last day.


Refunds
Sherlockapp.com says searches aren't refundable once they've run and prepaid periods aren't prorated, but it reviews technical failures and double charges. Sherlock Search points to your statutory rights and the store you paid through.


Who can use it
Both web versions require users to be 18+, ban stalking and harassment, and say results can't be used for employment, housing or credit decisions.




Two caveats apply to every face search tool, Sherlock included. First, results are possible matches: lookalikes are common, so open the source page and confirm with a second source before you act. Second, uploading someone else's photo has privacy consequences for them. Search with a real reason, such as checking a profile that's asking you for money, and never search photos of children.





  
  
  Five Checks Before You Pay for a Sherlock App



Check the developer or operator name on the store listing or checkout page — there's more than one "Sherlock".
Read the price and billing interval at checkout. Note whether it's weekly or monthly and when a trial ends.
Find the cancel path before you pay: your account page on the web, or App Store / Google Play subscriptions for apps.
Read the privacy policy for how long your photo is kept and whether it's sent to a third party.
Scan recent store reviews for complaints about searches that fail but still use up a credit, or charges after cancelling.
